phonemes.desc: Short open [a], stressed on the first syllable as in most Welsh words; the 'a' of 'cat' opened slightly.
Geminate alveolar nasal [nː], written double and held longer than a single English n.
The letter w is here a full vowel: short high back rounded [ʊ], the 'oo' of English 'put' — never a consonant.
Final alveolar nasal [n], closing the second syllable cleanly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AN-oon' — two syllables, stress on the first; the w is sounded as a short 'oo', so the name rhymes with 'cannon' said with Welsh vowels.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Annwfn, the spelling of the manuscripts — the f is the voiced [v] of lenited final -m, and the word was often understood as an- + dwfn, 'the deep, the abyss'

kin.label: Modern Welsh
kin.form: Annwn, the normalized modern spelling used since the modern period for the Otherworld of the Mabinogi

kin.label: Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru
kin.form: s.v. annwfn — 'the otherworld, the abyss'; the University of Wales dictionary records the form and its senses from the earliest poetry onward

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: an- (negative or intensifying prefix) + dwfn 'deep' — 'the un-deep, the very deep'; the popular reading 'not-world' is a later reinterpretation of the same sounds

pronunciation.note: Annwn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the realm's fame in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Otherworld, Underworld
domains.subtitle: The Deep, the Abyss — realm of the feast and the hunt
domains.lead: Annwn is the Welsh Otherworld of the Mabinogi and the oldest Welsh poetry — a realm of plenty where the feast never fails, ruled in the First Branch by [[arawn|Arawn]], and hunted across by Gwyn ap Nudd, whom God set over the demons of Annwn lest they destroy this world. Its cauldron, borne home from its fortresses at terrible cost, is the oldest quest of Arthurian tradition.

cards.name: The Cauldron of the Head of Annwn
cards.desc: Kindled by the breath of nine maidens, rimmed with pearls, it will not boil a coward's food — the prize of Arthur's voyage in Preiddeu Annwfn.

cards.name: The Hounds of Annwn
cards.desc: Arawn's pack — gleaming white with red ears, the colours the Welsh tradition gives every creature from the Otherworld.

cards.name: Prydwen
cards.desc: Arthur's ship on the voyage to the fortresses of Annwn — three full loads went in; except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.

cards.name: The Hunt of Gwyn ap Nudd
cards.desc: The son of Nudd rides with the hunt of Annwn; in Culhwch ac Olwen, God set him over its demons lest they destroy this world.

symbols.name: The cauldron of Pen Annwn
symbols.meaning: Plenty that will not serve the coward — abundance that answers only to courage

symbols.name: White hounds with red ears
symbols.meaning: The colours of the Otherworld made flesh — beauty that marks the boundary crossed

symbols.name: Caer Sidi and the fortresses
symbols.meaning: The revolving castle and its sister fortresses — the Otherworld as architecture that must be won, not visited

symbols.name: Prydwen
symbols.meaning: Arthur's ship — the voyage into the deep from which only seven returned

symbols.name: The year's exchange
symbols.meaning: Arawn and Pwyll trading shapes and kingdoms — the Otherworld close enough to wear a man's face

mythology.lead: Annwn is named in the very first pages of the Mabinogi and in the most difficult poem of early Welsh tradition. Its dossier is small and immense: a king who trades his shape, a cauldron that will not boil a coward's food, a hunt that keeps the world's demons leashed — and, behind all three, the deep itself.

myths.title: The Year in Annwn
myths.text:
Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, is hunting in Glyn Cuch when he drives a strange pack off a stag — hounds gleaming white, with red ears, the colours of the Otherworld — and feeds his own dogs on the kill. Their master rides up: [[arawn|Arawn]], a king of Annwn, and the offense is real. To make amends Pwyll accepts Arawn's bargain: for a year and a day they will exchange shapes and kingdoms, and at the year's end Pwyll must face Arawn's rival Hafgan — a king who can be killed by a single blow only; strike him twice and by the next day he fights as strongly as before.

Pwyll rules Annwn for the year in Arawn's likeness, in a court of unsurpassed plenty — and each night lies beside Arawn's queen without once touching her. At the appointed ford he strikes Hafgan once, refuses the second blow the wounded king begs for, and Annwn is united under Arawn. When the two kings meet again at Glyn Cuch and resume their own shapes, Arawn learns of the year's chastity and the friendship is sealed with gifts of horses, greyhounds, hawks, and gold. From that day Pwyll was called not Pwyll Prince of Dyfed but Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll, Head of Annwn.

myths.title: The Spoils of Annwn
myths.text:
The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwfn', preserved in the fourteenth-century Book of Taliesin and spoken in the poet's own voice, is the oldest surviving account of an Arthurian Otherworld raid. Arthur sails in his ship Prydwen against the fortresses of the deep — Caer Sidi, Caer Pedryfan, Caer Wydyr, and the rest — and the refrain tolls after each: 'except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.' Three full loads of Prydwen went into Annwn; seven men came back.

The prize is the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — kindled by the breath of nine maidens, its rim set about with pearls, and marked by the rule the Welsh tradition fixes on Otherworld vessels: it will not boil the food of a coward. The poem is elliptical, proud, and mournful at once — the poet stands apart from the swordsmen who went in and never came out — but its facts became permanent: the Otherworld has a cauldron, Arthur went to get it, and almost no one returned.

myths.title: Gwyn ap Nudd and the Demons of Annwn
myths.text:
The great hunting catalogue of Culhwch ac Olwen names its most uncanny huntsman: Gwyn ap Nudd, son of Nudd — 'God has set him over the demons of Annwn, lest this world be destroyed.' The hunt of the boar Twrch Trwyth cannot be accomplished without him, and so Gwyn rides out of Annwn at Arthur's muster: the Otherworld's own power, conscripted to keep its worst inhabitants leashed.

The same tale gives Gwyn his famous quarrel. He had carried off Creiddylad, daughter of Lludd, from her father's house, and Gwythyr ap Greidawl raised a host and took her back; Arthur judged between them — the maiden to remain with her father, and the two to fight for her every May Day until the Day of Judgment, when the winner takes her for good. Gwyn's hunt is therefore not seasonal sport but a standing order: Annwn's violence rides out under a king who is himself a covenant.

myths.title: The King on Glastonbury Tor
myths.text:
The Welsh Life of St Collen gives Annwn its most local address. Collen, keeping his hermitage under Glastonbury Tor, hears two men say that Gwyn ap Nudd — king of Annwn and of the Tylwyth Teg, the Fair Folk — holds his court above. Collen answers that the hosts of the air are demons; a summons follows, and on the summit he finds a castle of the utmost splendour, the king on a golden chair, and a banquet of dishes he has never seen the like of.

Collen sprinkles his holy water over the food, and the whole vision dissolves — castle, court, and king gone as if they had never been, leaving the saint standing on the green Tor. The tale is late and Christian, but it keeps the old facts in place: Gwyn is king of Annwn, his hall is a feast beyond earthly measure, and the Otherworld can open on a hillside in Somerset and close again without a trace.

lore.syncretism: Annwn's clearest kin are Irish: the síd of the Túatha Dé Danann, where the feast likewise never fails — the Dagda's cauldron of Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standing comparison for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and Mac Cana sets the two vessels side by side as one Celtic figure-type. The Irish Otherworld of the immrama and echtrai — Mag Mell, Emain Ablach, lands 'without grief, without sorrow, without death' — matches Annwn's profile point for point: plenty, beauty, and the suspension of age and sickness. Yet the Brythonic tradition is not a copy of the Gaelic one: no Irish text knows the name Annwn, and the Welsh corpus built its Otherworld on its own geography — the ford at Glyn Cuch, the revolving fortresses of the Taliesin poem, the Tor at Glastonbury. The Christian redactors left the structure intact while re-labelling its inhabitants: by Buchedd Collen, Gwyn ap Nudd's splendid court could be dismissed as a demonic glamour without surrendering one detail of the feast.
lore.culturalLegacy: Preiddeu Annwfn stands at the head of the Arthurian tradition: the raid on the Otherworld fortresses is older than every romance of the Grail, and scholars from Loomis onward have read the quest for the Head of Annwn's cauldron — a vessel of plenty that tests the worthy — as the Grail story's deepest Welsh root. The name kept working in Welsh: Annwn remains the living word for the Otherworld, and the white red-eared hounds became the Cŵn Annwn of later Welsh folklore, the pack whose crying in the night sky foretells a death. Gwyn ap Nudd rode out of the texts into modern Druidry and pagan practice as the great huntsman and psychopomp of the Welsh tradition, and Glastonbury Tor — crowned now by the stump of St Michael's tower — still carries his court in the popular imagination. Restoring Annwn in Unicode costs nothing and fixes something: the canonical spelling of the deep, held against the drift of anglicized spellings like Annwvyn and Annwyn.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Annwn is the rare Otherworld whose name tells you where it is: an- + dwfn, the un-deep, the very deep — not a land over the sea or under a hill but the depth beneath the world, the place the surface world is the skin of. The tradition never pretends it is far away. Pwyll stumbles into it on an ordinary hunt by breaking an ordinary courtesy; it lies a year's shape-shift away, close enough for two kings to trade faces and governments across it.

And its gifts all carry a price exacted in courage. The feast is boundless, but the cauldron will not boil a coward's food; the voyage is possible, but except seven none returned; the hunt rides out, but it rides to keep the demons of the deep leashed for the world's sake. Annwn is the Celtic imagination's answer to the question of what lies underneath: plenty without limit, behind a door that only opens once — and a word for it, five plain letters, that still means the deep.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh has been written in the Latin alphabet throughout its manuscript history, and the normalized form Annwn is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. The manuscripts spell the name Annwfn (Middle Welsh f writes the voiced [v]); the modern normalized spelling is Annwn. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: annwn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Annwn is a wholly textual realm: no inscription invokes it, and the Romano-British epigraphy of Wales is silent on the Otherworld by name. Its manuscript witnesses, however, are exact. The Mabinogi survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1400), the two great codices of medieval Welsh prose; Preiddeu Annwfn is preserved uniquely in the Book of Taliesin (National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century); and Culhwch ac Olwen comes down in a White Book fragment and the full Red Book text. The one site the tradition ties to Annwn is Glastonbury Tor, Gwyn ap Nudd's seat in Buchedd Collen: excavations on the Tor in the 1960s found sub-Roman and early medieval occupation beneath the ruins of St Michael's church — real archaeology on the hill, though none of it speaks to the Otherworld, whose only true location is the text.
